title: Strength Training During Pregnancy: The Guidance Is Clearer Than the Loading Details
subtitle: Major guidelines support strength activity in many uncomplicated pregnancies. The evidence is less precise about exactly how much to lift, how to progress, or what one person should change.
imageAlt: Two friends review a pregnancy training plan together beside a set of light dumbbells and resistance bands.
imageConcept: A warm, candid scene of two friends at home looking over a training log beside resistance bands and dumbbells, with one person leading the conversation and no emphasis on a particular body type or performance.
body:
“Can I lift?” sounds like one question, but it combines two different ones: whether strength activity is generally supported during pregnancy, and what training is appropriate for a particular person, pregnancy and moment. The first has a clearer answer. The second needs context. Treating them as interchangeable can make broad guidance sound like a personal clearance—or make uncertainty about specific loads sound like a reason everyone should stop.

For many people with uncomplicated pregnancies, strength-conditioning activity is part of the exercise conversation. That does not mean every program, movement or intensity is automatically suitable. The useful question is not simply whether lifting is allowed, but what a person currently does, how it feels, what has changed, and what their obstetric care provider advises for their circumstances.
What the broad guidance actually says

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists says people with uncomplicated pregnancies should be encouraged to do aerobic and strength-conditioning exercise. It also calls for clinical evaluation and careful consideration of complications or contraindications. In other words, the guidance supports activity as a category while leaving room for an individual assessment; it is not a universal training prescription or a promise that every exercise is right for every pregnancy [1].

That distinction matters for people who already lift, people who are new to strength training, and those whose access to care or training support differs. A general recommendation cannot account for a person’s health history, symptoms, previous training, available equipment or the advice they have received. If a question is specific to your own pregnancy, take it to your obstetric care provider rather than treating a guideline as personal clearance.
Why “how heavy?” is harder to answer

A recent systematic review and meta-analysis examined resistance training during pregnancy, drawing on 50 studies and 47,619 participants. Its scope makes it valuable for understanding the wider research, but the authors also identify limits that matter in the gym: many programs combined resistance work with other exercise, resistance-training doses were generally low to moderate, and researchers often reported the prescription and progression poorly [2].

So the number of participants should not be mistaken for a precise answer about a particular barbell load, repetition range or progression plan. If studies do not consistently describe sets, repetitions, intensity, external load and how training changed, it becomes harder to compare programs and draw detailed conclusions. Broad support for activity and uncertainty about exact loading can both be true. A careful article—or training decision—should keep those truths together.
A promising study is still a narrow study

One small study offers a useful example of what new evidence can and cannot establish. Researchers tested a single acute high-intensity resistance exercise session in 10 healthy pregnant participants, whose mean gestational age was 26.4±3.2 weeks. That is a specific group, at a particular point in pregnancy, completing one session—not a trial of every training style, every pregnancy circumstance or a program followed over time [3].

A study like this can add information about the session it examined. It cannot, on its own, establish that heavy lifting is appropriate for everyone, that the same approach is right throughout pregnancy, or that an individual should continue without changes. Headlines may flatten that distinction into “heavy lifting is safe” or “lifting is risky.” Neither is a responsible translation of a narrowly scoped study.
Make the conversation about your real week

A useful appointment question is more concrete than “Can I work out?” Bring a brief account of what you actually do: the movements or classes, how often you train, approximate session length, equipment, and what has recently changed. You do not need a perfect training log. A few clear notes can help your provider understand whether you mean a familiar routine, a new program, a particular lift or a change you have noticed.

Then ask about the decisions you need to make. For example: “I currently do these sessions; is there anything in my circumstances that changes the plan?” “Are there movements or intensities you want me to modify or pause?” “What changes or symptoms should prompt me to stop and contact you?” “When should we revisit this?” If you work with a coach, ask what information the provider is comfortable sharing with them. This keeps the conversation specific without asking a coach to make a medical assessment.
Adjustments can be practical, not dramatic

Pregnancy training does not have to be framed as either keeping everything exactly the same or abandoning strength work altogether. If a provider advises changes—or a familiar session no longer feels workable—discuss options in terms of the actual movement and the reason for the change. That might mean asking about a different variation, a lighter or otherwise adjusted effort, a shorter session, or pausing one element while you get guidance. These are examples to discuss, not a universal menu of medically approved modifications.

Make one change at a time when that is appropriate for your situation, and note what changed and how the session went. A simple record can include the exercise, the adjustment, and any relevant response. It is information to support a conversation, not a test you must pass or a way to diagnose what is happening. If a change brings a concern, pause the experiment and contact your care team for direction.

A plan made at one appointment is not necessarily a permanent contract. Pregnancy circumstances and a person’s experience of training can change; a sensible plan makes room to check in again. Agree on when to revisit the question, and clarify whom to contact if something changes before then. If you have more than one care professional involved, ask who should answer which questions so you are not left trying to reconcile conflicting advice alone.

This is also where access and preference matter. Someone may want to keep a familiar strength routine, find an alternative that fits available equipment, or take a break. The goal is not to prove commitment or achieve a particular performance standard. It is to make an informed choice with care that reflects the person’s circumstances and values.
Leave with a usable next step

The clearest takeaway is not a universal load or a rule to push through. Major guidance supports aerobic and strength-conditioning activity in many uncomplicated pregnancies, while the research on resistance-training dose and progression does not yet provide a detailed prescription that fits everyone. Bring your real routine and your specific questions to your obstetric care provider. Ask what applies to your circumstances, what should change, and when to check in again.

Before you leave the conversation, write down the agreed next step in plain language: continue a familiar activity while following the provider’s guidance, ask for clarification about a particular movement, or pause a question until you have more information. A useful strength plan is not the heaviest one or the most cautious one by default. It is one the person can understand, revisit and adapt with appropriate support.
